kaps_punt: Die Nylrivier en hoe dit nedersetting beïnvloed

items.bewering: Die Nyl se jaarlikse vloed het net die grond naby die rivier natgemaak.
items.blok: Die vloed was nie genoeg nie
items.bron: Britannica, Egypt: Land (via search extract) - the cultivated valley between Cairo and Aswan is about 8-16 km wide with desert beyond; WaterHistory.org, The Nile (excerpt from Postel, Pillar of Sand, 1999) - even a 2 m drop in flood level left up to a third of the floodplain unwatered, https://waterhistory.org/histories/nile. 'Naby die rivier' is relative (the floodplain can be several km wide) but not false.

items.bewering: Die water het ook net 'n deel van die jaar op die landerye gestaan.
items.blok: Die vloed was nie genoeg nie
items.bron: Wikipedia, Flooding of the Nile - basin fields were closed for about 45 days, then drained, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flooding_of_the_Nile; Library of Congress Country Study Egypt - flooding usually in August and September, https://countrystudies.us/egypt/89.htm.

items.bewering: Die res van die jaar was die landerye droog.
items.blok: Die vloed was nie genoeg nie
items.bron: Library of Congress Country Study Egypt: 'The floodwaters soaked the low-lying land, providing moisture for a single crop after they receded', https://countrystudies.us/egypt/89.htm; Wikipedia, Flooding of the Nile - water drained after about 45 days and 'sowing began immediately', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flooding_of_the_Nile; CIHEAM (search extract) - under the basin system the land lay fallow from about May to September. The fields were not dry for the whole rest of the year: the soaked soil carried the year's main crop for months after the water drained. They were dry in the hot months between harvest and the next flood. As written, a learner concludes that nothing could grow once the water left, which is the opposite of how the main crop grew.
items.regstelling: Ná die vloed het die deurweekte grond klam genoeg gebly vir een oes, maar in die warm maande voor die volgende vloed was die landerye droog.

items.bewering: Die vloed was ook nie elke jaar ewe groot nie.
items.blok: Die vloed was nie genoeg nie
items.bron: WaterHistory.org, The Nile - nilometers recorded each year's maximum flood level, low and high floods both occurred, https://waterhistory.org/histories/nile; Wikipedia, Ancient Egyptian agriculture (Nilometers section), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egyptian_agriculture.

items.bewering: Te min water het swak oeste en honger gebring, en te veel het dorpe en landerye beskadig.
items.blok: Die vloed was nie genoeg nie
items.bron: Wikipedia, Flooding of the Nile: 'If a flood was too large, it would damage villages, dykes and canals'; low floods meant upper basins could not be filled, 'food shortages or famine', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flooding_of_the_Nile; Wikipedia, Ancient Egyptian agriculture: 'Low flood levels could result in poor harvests and famine, while excessive flooding could damage settlements and agricultural land'; WaterHistory.org: 'A low flood could lead to famine'.

items.bewering: Die Egiptenare het kanale gegrawe om water na landerye verder van die rivier te lei.
items.bron: Encyclopedia.com, Irrigation Systems, Ancient - canals 'were used to flood large tracts of land while the Nile was flowing high', https://encyclopedia.com/science/news-wires-white-papers-and-books/irrigation-systems-ancient; Wikipedia, Flooding of the Nile - basin fields 'equipped with intake and exit canals'; Scorpion macehead (c. 3100 BC) read as a king opening an irrigation canal (search extracts). Note for the person: the canals worked within the floodplain, reaching basins the flood did not fill well on its own; the lesson does not claim they reached the desert, and should not.

items.bewering: Hulle het ook walle van grond rondom stukke land gebou. So 'n stuk land met walle rondom noem ons 'n kom.
items.bron: WaterHistory.org: 'a network of earthen banks, some parallel to the river and some perpendicular to it' formed basins of various sizes, https://waterhistory.org/histories/nile; Wikipedia, Ancient Egyptian agriculture: 'A crisscross network of earthen walls ... the water would be trapped in the basins formed by the walls'. 'Kom' is the lesson's Afrikaans for the English 'basin' and is defined in the text; no Afrikaans source for the term in this sense was found, but the concept it names is confirmed.

items.bewering: Die walle het die vloedwater weke lank vasgehou.
items.bron: WaterHistory.org: water held 'for a month or so until the soil was saturated'; Wikipedia, Flooding of the Nile: fields 'closed for about 45 days'. Both are weeks.

items.bewering: Ons noem dit besproeiing wanneer mense water so na hulle landerye lei.
items.bron: Vocabulary.com (Dutch 'besproeiing'): 'supplying dry land with water by means of ditches etc', https://www.vocabulary.com/dictionary/nl/besproeiing; Wikipedia, Ancient Egyptian agriculture and WaterHistory.org both call the Egyptian system 'basin irrigation'.

items.bewering: Later het boere ook 'n sjadoef gebruik om water op te lig.
items.bron: Wikipedia, Shadoof: appeared in Upper Egypt 'sometime after 2000 BC, most likely during the 18th Dynasty', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadoof; WaterHistory.org (Postel): appeared in Upper Egypt 'sometime after 1500 BC' and 'enabled farmers to irrigate crops near the river banks and canals during the dry summer'; tomb of Ipuy (TT217, Deir el-Medina, reign of Ramesses II) shows a shaduf in use (Met Museum facsimile 30.4.115, via search). Canals and basins go back to about 3100 BC, so 'later' holds. Eyre (Proc. British Academy 96, 1999, p. 34) notes the shaduf is attested from the New Kingdom in gardens and is 'not efficient' - consistent with the lesson, which makes no claim about scale.

items.bewering: Dit is 'n lang paal op 'n staander met 'n houer aan die een kant en 'n swaar gewig aan die ander kant.
items.bron: Wikipedia, Shadoof: 'an upright frame on which is suspended a long pole'; a bucket, skin bag or basket hangs from the long end; 'The short end carries a weight made of clay, stone, or a similar material'; Encyclopedia.com: 'a bucket ... from the long end of a pivoted boom, counterweighted at the short end'.

items.bewering: Dit werk soos 'n wipplank.
items.bron: Wikipedia, Shadoof: a counterbalanced lever on a pivot, the weight 'serves as the counterpoise of a lever'; Wikijunior How Things Work/Lever and JoVE (search extracts): a seesaw is a first-class lever with the pivot between the two loads. Mapping checked: pole on a pivot, one end goes down as the other goes up, the heavier side sinks - all carry over. The only difference is that a shaduf's pivot is off-centre (long arm for the bucket, short arm for the weight); a learner reasoning on from the seesaw is not led to anything false about how the shaduf lifts water.

items.bewering: Die boer trek die houer tot in die water af, en die gewig help om die vol houer op te lig.
items.bron: Wikipedia, Shadoof: the operator pulls the bucket down using body weight and the counterweight then lifts the full bucket.

items.bewering: Dan swaai hy die water oor na die kanaal of land.
items.bron: Wikipedia, Shadoof: 'At the end of each movement, the water is emptied out into runnels' that feed irrigation ditches; WaterHistory.org caption: 'A shaduf was used to raise water above the level of the Nile'.

items.bewering: Met kanale, komme en die sjadoef kon boere meer grond bewerk en genoeg kos vir 'n groeiende bevolking verbou.
items.bron: Tested as a set: each of the three extends cultivation. Canals flooded 'large tracts of land' (Encyclopedia.com); basins kept water on the land long enough to soak it (WaterHistory.org); the shaduf 'would have allowed the cultivated area to expand by 10-15 percent' (WaterHistory.org, excerpt from Postel, Pillar of Sand, 1999). Eyre (1999, p. 35) records 'a general trend of growth' to the New Kingdom; Haring, UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology 'Economy' (2009) cites Butzer's estimate of about 2.9 million people by about 1250 BC. Eyre calls the shaduf inefficient, which bears on how MUCH it added, not on whether it added land; the lesson makes no claim about scale. The three methods do distinct jobs (lead, hold, lift) and the lesson presents them without a false contrast.

items.bewering: Die Egiptenare het die rivier dus nie net gebruik nie maar ook leer beheer.
items.bron: WaterHistory.org: basin irrigation was 'an enhancement of the natural hydrological patterns of the Nile River, not a wholesale transformation of them'; 'complete control of the river' came only with modern irrigation and flood works, https://waterhistory.org/histories/nile; Eyre, 'The Village Economy in Pharaonic Egypt', Proc. British Academy 96 (1999), p. 34: Pharaonic Egypt 'was not in a straightforward sense an artificial irrigation society'; the main issue was how far natural flooding was subject to local intervention; Wikipedia, Flooding of the Nile: flood height could only be forecast short-term. The Egyptians could not control how high the river rose - the lesson's own first block says too much water damaged villages and fields. What they controlled was where the floodwater went once it came, and how long it stayed.
items.regstelling: Die Egiptenare het die rivier dus nie net gebruik nie, maar ook geleer om sy water te lei en vas te hou waar hulle dit nodig gehad het. (Narrow the object from 'die rivier' to its water; do not claim they controlled the river or its flood.)

items.bewering: besproeiing: Om water na gewasse te lei wanneer daar te min reën val.
items.bron: Vocabulary.com: 'supplying dry land with water by means of ditches etc'; Merriam-Webster's 'canal' entry lists irrigating land as a purpose of artificial waterways. 'Wanneer daar te min reën val' is the usual reason and fits Egypt, where crops relied on the Nile rather than rain.

items.bewering: kanaal: 'n Sloot wat mense grawe om water na 'n ander plek te lei.
items.bron: Merriam-Webster and Dictionary.com (search extracts): a canal is an artificial waterway for boats, drainage or irrigation. The entry gives the irrigation sense only; that is incomplete (shipping canals exist) but not false, and it is the sense this lesson uses.

items.bewering: kom: 'n Stuk land met walle van grond rondom wat water vashou.
items.bron: WaterHistory.org and Wikipedia, Ancient Egyptian agriculture: basins were areas enclosed by earthen banks that trapped the floodwater.

items.bewering: sjadoef: 'n Lang paal met 'n houer en 'n swaar gewig waarmee boere water oplig.
items.bron: Wikipedia, Shadoof (structure and use as above).

items.bewering: staander: 'n Regop paal of raam wat iets anders dra.
items.bron: Wiktionary, staander (Dutch, the same word): 'support beam, stand (vertical support of any kind)', https://en.wiktionary.com/wiki/staander; Wikipedia, Shadoof: the pole hangs on 'an upright frame'. No Afrikaans dictionary entry was reached online (WAT not returned by search); the Dutch sense matches the definition and the lesson's use.

items.bewering: bevolking: Al die mense wat in 'n land of plek woon.
items.bron: Merriam-Webster, population: 'the whole number of people or inhabitants in a country or region'; Dictionary.com: 'the total number of people inhabiting a country, city, or any district or area'.

opsomming: Two claims overstate and need narrowing - the fields were not dry for the whole rest of the year (the soaked soil carried the main crop for months), and the Egyptians learned to steer and hold the Nile's floodwater, not to control the river itself, which the lesson's own first block contradicts; everything else checks out, the three methods hold as a set, the seesaw comparison maps correctly, and the lesson contains no superlatives.
